content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Deadlocks: Detection, Prevention, and Resolution in Database Design"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In relational database management systems (RDBMS), concurrency is essential for handling multiple transactions simultaneously. However, concurrent execution introduces the risk of race conditions and deadlocks. A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are permanently blocked because each transaction holds a lock on a resource that the other transaction requires."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Four Necessary Conditions for Deadlocks"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"For a deadlock to occur in a database system, four conditions (known as the Coffman conditions) must hold simultaneously:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Hold and Wait: A transaction is currently holding at least one resource and requesting additional resources that are being held by other transactions."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a transaction; they can only be released voluntarily by the transaction holding them."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Circular Wait: A closed chain of transactions exists, such that each transaction holds one or more resources that are needed by the next transaction in the chain."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Deadlock Prevention Strategies"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Prevention strategies ensure that at least one of the four deadlock conditions can never be satisfied during database operations."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Resource Ordering: Enforce a global ordering on all database resources. Transactions must request locks in a predefined sequential order, which breaks the circular wait condition."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"All-Or-Nothing Allocation: Require transactions to acquire all necessary locks at once before execution begins. If any lock is unavailable, the transaction acquires none and waits."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Deadlock Detection and Resolution"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Instead of preventing deadlocks, many modern databases allow them to happen and use detection mechanisms. The database engine periodically constructs a Wait-For Graph (WFG), where nodes represent transactions and directed edges represent resource dependency."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"Transaction 1 -> holds Lock A, requests Lock B\nTransaction 2 -> holds Lock B, requests Lock A\n[Wait-For Graph Cycle Detected: T1 -> T2 -> T1]"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a cycle is detected in the Wait-For Graph, the database management system initiates deadlock resolution by choosing a victim transaction to abort. The victim is typically selected based on criteria such as the minimum amount of work done, fewest locks held, or youngest transaction age."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Developers"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Keep transactions as short as possible to minimize the window of lock contention."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Access objects in the same order across different application modules and queries."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Implement application-level retry logic to gracefully handle transaction rollbacks triggered by deadlocks (e.g., catching error code 1213 in MySQL)."}]
